text: You've checked whether individual vectors are unit length and whether pairs of vectors are orthogonal. This lesson puts both ideas to work at once — a basis that's simultaneously all of those things — and introduces the operator that does exactly what 'picking out one component' means in quantum mechanics.

A set of vectors is an orthonormal basis if every vector has inner product 1 with itself, and every distinct pair has inner product 0. Testing e1 equals one over root 2, times 1,1, and e2 equals one over root 2, times 1, negative 1 — the same two columns as the Hadamard matrix — all three checks pass: each has norm 1, and the two are orthogonal to each other.

An outer product, written ket-a bra-b, builds a matrix instead of a number. The projection operator onto ket-zero is ket-zero bra-zero, which works out entry by entry to 1,0,0,0 — a matrix with a very specific job: keep only the amount of ket-zero in a vector and zero out everything else.

Take psi equals 0.6, 0.8i — already confirmed normalized. Applying the projection gives 0.6, 0 — the ket-one part is zeroed out, and the ket-zero part passes through unchanged. That result is exactly the inner product of ket-zero and psi, which is 0.6, times ket-zero itself — the general pattern every projection follows.

When a qubit is measured in the standard basis, the projection operators ket-zero bra-zero and ket-one bra-one are exactly the objects that isolate each possible outcome's component, and the squared magnitude of that projected amplitude gives the measurement probability. This only works cleanly when you're projecting onto an orthonormal basis — otherwise the projections would double-count part of the state, and the outcome probabilities wouldn't add up to 1.

Next lesson is a problem-solving lab: four fresh problems that put an inner product, a Hermitian check, a unitary check, and a probability-style inner product all to work on numbers you haven't seen before.
